endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Provide all patients, no later than the date of first service delivery, with a comprehensive Notice of Privacy Practices (NPP), including how protected health information (PHI) may be used by AI solutions, in compliance with HIPAA.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Implement plans for GAI systems to undergo regular adversarial testing to identify vulnerabilities and potential manipulation or misuse.

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Assess training of new end users

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: this assessment may include, for example, evaluation of the 1896 training program intended for risk control.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Evaluate whether assigned roles and responsibilities foster transparency and trust in the AI system and whether adherence to roles and understanding of the system among users and stakeholders can be measured.

endorsements.title: AI literacy among healthcare professionals and students in the Americas
endorsements.quote: Periodic assessments of effectiveness — through pre- and post-intervention testing, learner feedback, and curricular benchmarking — are critical to refine these approaches and guarantee that training formats are both pedagogically sound and institutionally sustainable.

evidence.title: Evaluating Training Effectiveness for a Technology-Driven Pain Assessment Application: A Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.venue: Pain management nursing : official journal of the American Society of Pain Management Nurses
evidence.outcome: Post-training knowledge check identifying competency gaps
evidence.effect: Knowledge survey showed correct scores ranging from 36.8% to 84.2%, identifying a need for further education.
evidence.quote: Staff's correct knowledge scores varied (36.8% to 84.2%), indicating a need for further education.

commentary.bottom_line: One small descriptive study found that a post-training knowledge check among 19 clinical staff produced correct scores ranging from 36.8% to 84.2%, which suggests that such checks can reveal competency gaps. No study tested whether periodic assessment improves user competency, AI use, or patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: The only test is a single cross-sectional study of 19 nurses and physiotherapists in a simulated setting in Australia. It shows that a knowledge check detected variable scores, but it has no comparison group, measures no downstream effect, and is imprecise. Certainty is very low. Case scenarios and audits of user actions were not studied.

Scores as low as 36.8% after training suggest that some users may finish training without adequate understanding of the tool. A knowledge check may flag these users before they rely on AI output with patients, but the study did not track errors or harm, so the safety benefit remains unmeasured.

The study used a knowledge survey in an offline or simulated setting, which tells us little about how users behave with AI in live workflows. Audits of actual user actions against intended use would address that gap, yet no study examined their fidelity, burden, or effect on practice.

FUTURE-AI advises assessing training of new end users, and the CHAI assurance guide asks whether user understanding can be measured. FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled devices states that assessment may include evaluation of a training program used for risk control. Two cited framework excerpts, on privacy notices and adversarial testing, do not address training assessment.

commentary.research_gap: Controlled or pre-post studies in live clinical settings should test whether periodic knowledge checks, case scenarios, and audits of user actions change AI use, error rates, or patient outcomes, and should report the staff time and cost of running these assessments.
commentary.underserved_note: The single study enrolled 19 clinical staff in Australia and did not report on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Health systems serving these populations have no evidence on whether competency assessment works for their staff or protects their patients.
